question: An API that verifies an RS256 bearer token on every request and then reads or writes one row: how much mixed traffic does one core carry, in each runtime?

estimator.capacity: the highest rate on the grid that met the service level in a majority of the repetitions
estimator.operatingPoint: the measured window at that rate which met the service level
estimator.latency: clientP99 is latency-corrected (it includes time a request was due but not yet sent); serverP99 is time to first byte. Where they part company, the generator was falling behind the schedule the service could no longer keep.
estimator.floorAndDbCeiling: best of the repetitions (upper bounds on a host that cannot be quiesced)
estimator.soak: first window dropped; it carries the cost of a pool that has just opened
estimator.serviceLevel: both halves of the mix at >= 99% of target, p99 <= 10 ms, no failed request

read.what: token verification (scope events:read), then one row by primary key out of the seeded 1,000,000

write.what: token verification (scope events:write), JSON body validation, then one INSERT ... RETURNING id

slo.note: A rate counts as carried only if both halves of the mix arrive at >= 99% of their target and both stay under the p99 budget, with no non-2xx answer and no transport error.

tune.note: Closed loop, flat out, two repetitions, best of the two. Each candidate gets the pool size that carried the most mixed traffic at that core budget; the whole table is kept so the choice can be checked. Best rather than median for the same reason the ceiling phase of bench/run.sh uses it: the host is a laptop that cannot be quiesced, and interference only ever subtracts. Flat out the two halves do not hold the 50/50 ratio — reads are cheaper, so more of them get through. That is fine for ranking pool sizes, which is all this phase decides.

floor.note: An nginx that runs no application code, on the same cores as the candidate. Nothing that parses a token can beat it.

dbCeiling.note: pgbench inserting the same row shape straight into PostgreSQL, with no HTTP and no token in the way: where the database itself stops, and therefore where a comparison between the runtimes would stop meaning anything. pgbench needs enough threads of its own (-j) not to become the limit it is measuring.
